paragraphs.text: [Rougui](yancha:rougui), cassia in Chinese, is a cultivar of the [Wuyi Mountains](wuyi-mountains:where-it-is), the range along the border of northern Fujian and Jiangxi. It dates from the Qing dynasty and is now one of the most widely planted teas in the area. The bushes there grow in [thin, stony soil](wuyi-mountains:nature) on ledges, in ravines and between rocks. The ground drains fast and mist settles on the slopes, which is why growth on the mountain is slow.

This leaf was made in the standard way for [Wuyi rock tea](yancha:definition). It was withered and rested, then twisted into long thin strips rather than rolled into balls, and finished with a [charcoal roast](yancha:making). The roast is done in several rounds, with rests of weeks or months between them, not in one pass. It dries the tea so that it keeps, and each stage has to be managed with care.

brewing.text: Wuyi tea is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C, and about 5 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 120 ml gaiwan, a third to a half full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 5 to 20 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and good rock tea gives seven steeps or more. In a larger pot, use about 2 to 5 grams for 250 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: Roast and stone fruit, a mineral, rocky texture and a long, sweet, mouth-watering finish. Light roast is bright and floral, medium roast fruity and rounded, full roast charcoal, wood and roasted nuts. Da Hong Pao is often floral, Rougui spicy with cinnamon, young Shui Xian sweet and smooth, and old-bush Shui Xian woody and mossy.
